bug_report: The rollout order for yesterday's release looked random - a dependent service went out before the thing it reads from, and the checkout blip during release is back. A failing repro is at tests/test_regression.py. Fix plan_waves so a service never rolls out ahead of what it depends on, without breaking existing behaviour.

conversations.text: Yesterday's release order looked random again - the checkout blip is back, and at least one service went out before the thing it reads from had even started rolling. The release channel was not amused.

plan_waves currently returns the whole fleet as one alphabetical batch, so ordering is pure luck. I'll switch it to dependency leveling: a service deploys in the wave after its dependencies, and inside a wave I'll keep it alphabetical by name.

Leveling is right, with one precision: a service goes in the wave AFTER its DEEPEST dependency - it waits for the last of its deps, not the first. But alphabetical inside a wave is not enough and I don't want it shipped that way: every service has a tier field, 0 being the most critical. Inside a wave it's tier ascending - tier 0 rolls first - and name A-Z only as the tiebreak, so the plan stays deterministic.
Deepest dep for the level, tier-then-name within the wave. While I'm in the planner: do you want a dry-run mode that prints the waves without deploying, for the release channel?

The deploy driver already has --plan-only; keep plan_waves a pure function that returns lists of names, the tooling does the formatting. And a heads-up: the waves integration test has been flaky on CI - the timing assertion around the mock deployer - rerun before assuming your change did it.
Understood. Question about the deps data: some services list dependencies that aren't part of the release at all - shared infra like the message bus. Should those count for leveling?

Ignore any dep the planner can't resolve among the services it's leveling - that's external infra, it's already running, it gates nothing. Level only within the release. Next thing you'll hit in the data is the canary flag on some services - that one changes the plan, so ask before guessing.

I see it - canary: true on a couple of services. My instinct: keep each canary in its leveled wave but move it to the front WITHIN that wave, so it goes first among its peers without violating dependency order.

No - that buries the canaries mid-release, which defeats the point of having them. Canaries don't participate in the leveling at all: they form their own wave at the very front, wave 0, before everything else, whatever their dependencies say.
Even a canary that depends on a service deploying two waves later? That deliberately inverts the dependency order for it.

Deliberately, yes - ops decision from the last release retro. The canaries exist to validate the release before anything else rolls, and their dependencies are assumed already live from the previous release; if a canary's dep is actually down, the canary failing IS the early signal we want. Order the canary wave by name.
OK. When a release has no canaries, should I emit an empty wave 0 anyway so wave indexes stay stable across releases for the dashboards?
No empty leading wave - with no canaries the first leveled wave is simply first. The dashboard keys waves by content, not by index, so don't pad.
One review nit on the output shape: today it returns lists of names. Keep that, or return the full service dicts per wave?

Names only, as today - three tools parse that output and none of them want dicts. For rollout, regenerate the plans for the last three releases and diff them against what actually shipped; release-eng reviews the deltas before the next real rollout uses the new planner.

Final wave policy: services marked canary form wave 0, always first, ordered by name - their dependencies are assumed already live from the previous release; every other service deploys in the wave after its DEEPEST in-release dependency, with unresolvable deps ignored; within a wave, tier ascending - tier 0 most critical first - then name A-Z as the tiebreak; and when there are no canaries there is no empty leading wave. plan_waves stays a pure function returning lists of names.

policy: waves by dependency depth; within a wave tier asc then name; canary services always wave 0 (deps assumed already live)
non_guessable: waves by dependency depth; within a wave tier asc then name; canary services always wave 0 (deps assumed already live)
